(Horrible example, but you get it right?)

I split it into two versions - individual honour and societal honour

Individual honour, to me, means doing what you'll say you'll do, going out of your way to help someone even if you don't know them, trying not to be destructive, trying to make good changes where you can, and trying to emphasise honesty over deception.

Societal honour is the more twisted version. To me, it's always been about powerful people convincing the less powerful that sacrificing themselves for the elite is a way to earn respect and glory. I'm not a historian, but when I think of oaths of fealty to lords, committing suicide if it is politically convenient for your liege lord (in the older Japanese context), and even in the modern world, pledging to die for someone else's interests in war, it makes me view that kind of honour very sceptically.

Even now you can see people self-sacrificing to gain societal honour from elites (in much less life-or-death ways). Workers who volunteer for unpaid overtime, who put off vacations, who work through illness, who sacrifice their own happiness for the organisation - they're often highlighted by the corporate hierarchy as honourable people to be emulated.

Self-sacrifice is an amazing thing in a life or death situation or when you're a tribe fighting for survival, but when self-sacrifice just leads to larger profits the worker doesn't share, it seems pointless. When it comes down to it, the company doesn't care about the worker, and they can't cash in their accrued societal honour unless it's for small promotions or pay rises.

Half of the concept of honour seems really admirable and worth emulating; the other half seems like an efficient system dating back thousands of years that helps people in charge make the less powerful voluntarily give up their own agency for someone else's benefit.
